y-m-62-01.title: Are the limit value and the function value the same thing? Checking a solution
y-m-62-01.topic: Telling apart left-hand and right-hand limits and the function value
y-m-62-01.goal: By finding the error in a solution, confirm that even when the function value is defined at x=2, it is separate from the limit value, and that if the left-hand and right-hand limits differ, there is no limit.
y-m-62-01.material: Define the function f like this (x is a real number). If x is less than 2, f(x)=x+1; if x=2, f(2)=5; if x is greater than 2, f(x)=x squared minus 1 (x²−1). The function g is: if x is less than 2, g(x)=x+1; if x=2, g(2)=3; if x is greater than 2, g(x)=x squared (x²). A student wrote a solution finding the limit of f as x goes to 2 as below.
y-m-62-01.thinking.0: Check the grounds for each line of the solution
y-m-62-01.thinking.1: Tell apart the limit value and the function value
y-m-62-01.thinking.2: Judge the conclusion when the left-hand and right-hand limits differ
y-m-62-01.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-01.prereq.1: The meaning of the limit of a function (the value f(x) approaches as x approaches a)
y-m-62-01.prereq.2: The meaning of the left-hand and right-hand limit notation (x approaches a from the side less than a and from the side greater than a)
y-m-62-01.prereq.3: Calculating limit values of polynomial functions (substitution)
y-m-62-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in the student's solution whose grounds are wrong.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, mark whether the value used is one obtained where x is not 2, or the value when x=2.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put the results of lines 3 and 4 side by side with the conclusion of line 5 and compare.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.line.1: When x approaches 2, x is not 2, so use f(x)=x+1 on the side less than 2 and f(x)=x²−1 on the greater side.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.line.2: Going to 2 from the left: the limit of x+1 is 3.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.line.3: Going to 2 from the right: the limit of x²−1 is 3.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.line.4: The left-hand and right-hand limits are the same, so the limit exists, and its value is f(2)=5.
y-m-62-01.s.s1.explain: Line 5 is wrong. In lines 3 and 4, the left-hand and right-hand limits are both 3, so the limit exists and its value is 3. The limit value is determined by the values while x approaches 2, and the function value f(2)=5 at x=2 does not enter that calculation. So for this function the limit value 3 and the function value 5 are different.
y-m-62-01.s.s2.prompt: Now look at the function g. g(2)=3. Choose the most appropriate explanation about the limit of g as x goes to 2.
y-m-62-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write separately the values g(x) approaches from the side where x is less than 2 and the side where it is greater.
y-m-62-01.s.s2.hint.1: First compare whether the two values are the same, and then look at g(2).
y-m-62-01.s.s2.o.a: The function value g(2)=3 equals the left-hand limit 3, so the limit value is 3
y-m-62-01.s.s2.r.a: You decided the limit just because one left-side value equals the function value. Did you check the value approached from the right?
y-m-62-01.s.s2.o.b: The average 3.5 of the left-hand limit 3 and the right-hand limit 4 is the limit value
y-m-62-01.s.s2.r.b: When the two values differ, you took the middle value as the limit. A limit must gather at one value, so look again at the situation where the left and right go to different values.
y-m-62-01.s.s2.o.c: The left-hand limit is 3 and the right-hand limit is 4, so they differ and the limit does not exist at x=2
y-m-62-01.s.s2.o.d: g(2) is defined as 3, so the limit value is 3
y-m-62-01.s.s2.r.d: You treated the limit value and the function value as the same thing. Recall that for f the limit value 3 and the function value 5 were different.
y-m-62-01.s.s2.explain: g approaches 3 from the left and 4 from the right. If the left-hand and right-hand limits differ, then even though g(2) is defined, the limit as x goes to 2 does not exist.
y-m-62-01.s.s3.prompt: For g, even though the function value g(2) exists, there was no limit. Using g as an example, write in one or two sentences how a limit and a function value are different concepts.
y-m-62-01.s.s3.hint.0: You can use the two numbers you used for the left-hand and right-hand limits of g as they are.
y-m-62-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write two sentences side by side in the form 'The limit is the value when ..., and the function value is the value at ...'.
y-m-62-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The limit is ..., and the function value is ...
y-m-62-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the limit is the value as x approaches 2, not the value at the point x=2 itself?
y-m-62-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use the numbers of the left-hand and right-hand limits of g (3 and 4) as grounds?
y-m-62-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid saying that a limit must exist just because a function value exists?
y-m-62-01.s.s3.model.0: A limit is the value g(x) approaches as x approaches 2, and the function value g(2) is the actual value at x=2. Even if g(2)=3, the right-hand limit is 4, so the left and right differ and there is no limit.
y-m-62-01.s.s3.model.1: The function value is the value at that point, and a limit exists only if the values approached from the left and right are the same, so they are separate. g goes to 3 from the left and 4 from the right, so even though g(2)=3 exists, the limit does not exist.

y-m-62-02.title: How many pairs (a, b) make it continuous?
y-m-62-02.topic: Continuity and differentiability of piecewise-defined functions
y-m-62-02.goal: Using examples you build yourself, confirm that there are infinitely many, not just one, coefficient pairs that make a piecewise function continuous at x=1, and judge how the pairs that are also differentiable are different.
y-m-62-02.material: For constants a and b, define the function f as follows (x is a real number). If x is less than 1, f(x)=x squared plus a times x (x²+ax), and if x is at least 1, f(x)=2x+b. Below, a and b are independent constants.
y-m-62-02.thinking.0: Compare the number of unknowns and the number of conditions
y-m-62-02.thinking.1: Build several solutions and check the conditions
y-m-62-02.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-02.prereq.1: The condition for a function to be continuous at x=a (left-hand limit = right-hand limit = function value)
y-m-62-02.prereq.2: Differentiating polynomial functions (x squared, linear expressions)
y-m-62-02.prereq.3: The meaning of the derivative (the slopes on the left and right must be equal for it to be differentiable)
y-m-62-02.s.s1.prompt: How many pairs (a, b) are there that make f continuous at x=1? Before starting calculations, choose the most appropriate judgment.
y-m-62-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write the values you get by plugging x=1 into the left expression and the right expression at x=1.
y-m-62-02.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many equations in a and b the condition that the two values are equal gives.
y-m-62-02.s.s1.o.a: There is only one pair, for which both a and b are determined
y-m-62-02.s.s1.r.a: You thought that since there are two unknowns the values are determined as one. Count how many equations the continuity gives.
y-m-62-02.s.s1.o.b: a and b are determined as two different pairs
y-m-62-02.s.s1.r.b: Check where the grounds for two pairs came from. Look at how many equations there are and of what degree.
y-m-62-02.s.s1.o.c: The expression differs for each interval, so there is no pair that makes it continuous
y-m-62-02.s.s1.r.c: You thought that since the expression differs for each interval, they can't be joined. Compare the values of the two expressions at x=1 directly.
y-m-62-02.s.s1.o.d: There is only one equation, so choosing a determines b
y-m-62-02.s.s1.explain: For it to be continuous at x=1, the left-hand limit 1+a and the function value (right-hand limit) 2+b must be equal. There is only this one equation, so b=a−1, and if you choose a freely, b is determined.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.prompt: Make three different pairs (a, b) of integers that are continuous at x=1, with the absolute value of a at most 4.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.hint.0: First pick one a and find the value of the left expression at x=1.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.hint.1: Adjust b so that it equals the value of the right expression.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The left-hand limit 1+a and the right-hand limit (function value) 2+b are equal.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.fail.c1: At x=1, the value of the left expression 1+a and the value of the right expression 2+b are not equal.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.fail.c2: a and b must be integers.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The absolute value of a is at most 4.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The absolute value of a is greater than 4.
y-m-62-02.s.s2.explain: It is continuous if b=a−1 holds. Examples: (0, −1), (2, 1), (−3, −4). If a is the same, b is the same too, so to count different pairs, a must differ.
y-m-62-02.s.s3.prompt: Among the pairs you just made, choose the correct statement about the pairs that are also differentiable at x=1. (To be differentiable at x=1, the derivatives from the left and from the right must be equal.)
y-m-62-02.s.s3.hint.0: Differentiate the expression for the side where x is less than 1 and find the value at x=1.
y-m-62-02.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether there is an a that makes it equal to the slope of the right expression.
y-m-62-02.s.s3.o.a: Among the continuous pairs, only the pair a=0, b=−1 is differentiable
y-m-62-02.s.s3.o.b: If it is continuous it is differentiable, so all the pairs you made qualify
y-m-62-02.s.s3.r.b: You thought that continuous means differentiable. Find the slopes on the left and right separately and compare them.
y-m-62-02.s.s3.o.c: None of the continuous pairs is differentiable
y-m-62-02.s.s3.r.c: You reached a conclusion without comparing the slopes. See whether there is an a for which the left slope 2+a and the right slope 2 are equal.
y-m-62-02.s.s3.o.d: The larger a is, the more differentiable it becomes
y-m-62-02.s.s3.r.d: When a gets larger, the left slope 2+a also gets larger and moves away from the right 2. Look for the value where the slopes are equal.
y-m-62-02.s.s3.explain: At x=1, the left derivative is 2·1+a=2+a and the right derivative is 2. For them to be equal, a=0, and from the continuity condition b=−1. Even if it is continuous, most pairs bend at x=1, so they are not differentiable.

y-m-62-03.title: If the sign changes, can we say there is a root?
y-m-62-03.topic: Conditions for using the Intermediate Value Theorem
y-m-62-03.goal: Judge that continuity is a condition needed to apply the Intermediate Value Theorem, and tell apart the existence of a root from the statement that there is exactly one root.
y-m-62-03.material: The only things known about the function f are f(1)=−2 and f(3)=4. Mina said, "So there must be an x between 1 and 3 with f(x)=0." Junho asked, "We don't know whether the graph is continuous, so can we say that for sure?"
y-m-62-03.thinking.0: Judge whether the given information leads to a conclusion
y-m-62-03.thinking.1: Find the line in an argument that goes too far
y-m-62-03.thinking.2: Say what information is needed to make the conclusion stronger
y-m-62-03.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-03.prereq.1: The meaning of continuity of a function
y-m-62-03.prereq.2: The Intermediate Value Theorem: for f continuous on a closed interval [a, b], f takes any value k between f(a) and f(b) at some c (as understood by students who know it)
y-m-62-03.prereq.3: The meaning of open and closed intervals
y-m-62-03.s.s1.prompt: How should we judge Mina's statement (there must be an x between 1 and 3 with f(x)=0) from only the information written above?
y-m-62-03.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether you can draw a graph that passes through f(1)=−2 and f(3)=4 but never passes through 0.
y-m-62-03.s.s1.hint.1: Say what must happen to the graph for such a graph to be possible.
y-m-62-03.s.s1.o.a: f(1) is negative and f(3) is positive, so there must be one
y-m-62-03.s.s1.r.a: You asserted it from the fact that the sign changes alone. Think about whether there are functions whose values skip over the middle.
y-m-62-03.s.s1.o.b: We can't tell whether it is continuous, so we can't assert it from this information
y-m-62-03.s.s1.o.c: If f(1) and f(3) have different signs, there cannot be a root
y-m-62-03.s.s1.r.c: You treated different signs as grounds for there being no root. Recall a scene where a continuous graph changes sign.
y-m-62-03.s.s1.o.d: We can say there must be one only when f is an increasing function
y-m-62-03.s.s1.r.d: You thought a monotonic condition is needed. Check what happens for a continuous function that is not increasing when the sign changes.
y-m-62-03.s.s1.explain: The Intermediate Value Theorem can be used when f is continuous on a closed interval. If we don't know that it is continuous, the values can skip over 0, so we can't say there must be one. It does not need to be an increasing function.
y-m-62-03.s.s2.prompt: The following is the argument of a student who assumed that f is continuous on [1, 3]. Choose the line that makes an overreaching conclusion.
y-m-62-03.s.s2.hint.0: Compare whether lines 3 and 4 each say 'at least one' or 'exactly one'.
y-m-62-03.s.s2.hint.1: Draw whether a graph that crosses the x-axis upward, then downward, and then upward again is possible.
y-m-62-03.s.s2.line.0: Assumption: f is continuous on the closed interval [1, 3].
y-m-62-03.s.s2.line.2: By the Intermediate Value Theorem, there is at least one c in the open interval (1, 3) with f(c)=0.
y-m-62-03.s.s2.line.3: The sign changes once, so the graph crosses the x-axis only once, and there is exactly one such c.
y-m-62-03.s.s2.line.4: Therefore the equation f(x)=0 has a real root in (1, 3).
y-m-62-03.s.s2.explain: Line 4 goes too far. With the assumption of continuity alone, we can say that there is at least one c with f(c)=0, but we can't know that there is exactly one. For example, f(x)=(10/3)(x−1.5)(x−2)(x−2.2) has f(1)=−2 and f(3)=4 and is continuous, but has three roots, 1.5, 2, and 2.2.
y-m-62-03.s.s3.prompt: If in addition to f being continuous you knew one more piece of information, could you say that 'there is exactly one x in (1, 3) with f(x)=0'? Write it with your reason.
y-m-62-03.s.s3.hint.0: Say what kind of movement is needed for the graph to cross the x-axis several times.
y-m-62-03.s.s3.hint.1: Find what property prevents that movement from happening.
y-m-62-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If we know f is ..., then ... so
y-m-62-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is the extra information I wrote new information separate from being continuous?
y-m-62-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why, with that information, there cannot be two or more roots?
y-m-62-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you consider whether other extra information (for example, knowing it is a quadratic) is also possible?
y-m-62-03.s.s3.model.0: If we know f is always increasing on (1, 3), then once the value passes through 0 it can't become 0 again, so there is only one root.
y-m-62-03.s.s3.model.1: If we know the derivative f′(x) is always positive on (1, 3), then f is increasing, so the graph crosses the x-axis only once and there is exactly one root.

y-m-62-04.title: If the limit of a slope measured symmetrically exists, is it differentiable?
y-m-62-04.topic: The definition of the derivative and the symmetric difference
y-m-62-04.goal: Using a counterexample, confirm that even if the 'limit of the symmetric difference' exists at x=a, the derivative does not necessarily exist, and tell apart the two directions of the statement.
y-m-62-04.material: Jinwoo's claim: "If the quotient (f(a+h)−f(a−h))/(2h) has a limit as h goes to 0, then f is differentiable at x=a." (How to read: f of a plus h minus f of a minus h, divided by 2h.) The data below is given one step at a time. At each step, choose your thought about the claim.
y-m-62-04.thinking.0: Know the limits of judging a general statement from one example
y-m-62-04.thinking.1: Change your judgment with new data
y-m-62-04.thinking.2: Look separately at whether the converse direction holds
y-m-62-04.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-04.prereq.1: The definition of the derivative (the limit as h→0 of the quotient (f(a+h)−f(a))/h)
y-m-62-04.prereq.2: The meaning of the absolute value function |x|
y-m-62-04.s.s1.prompt: Looking at the data, choose your thought about Jinwoo's claim at each step.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write in one word whether the newly given data supports the claim, shakes it, or makes you hold off on judging.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.hint.1: At step 3, write with an arrow which direction the claim goes ('the limit exists ⇒ differentiable'), and also write the opposite direction separately to compare.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.info: For f(x)=x² and a=1, (f(1+h)−f(1−h))/(2h) = ((1+h)²−(1−h)²)/(2h) = 4h/(2h) = 2. This limit is 2, and f′(1) found by the definition is also 2.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: After seeing this data, what do you think of Jinwoo's claim?
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.after: For x², the two values were the same. But one example cannot settle a general statement, so 'it may be right but needs more testing' is appropriate.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: One example was right, so we confirm that it holds for all functions
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You confirmed a general statement from one correct example. Whether it holds for any function needs to be tested with other examples.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is right in this example, but we need to check more whether it also holds for other functions
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The same value coming out is a coincidence, so the claim is already wrong
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You treated the same value coming out as a coincidence without any grounds. The fact that the same value came out is also information.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The claim seems possibly right, but it is too early to confirm it from this example alone
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.info: For f(x)=|x| and a=0, when h is not 0, (f(h)−f(−h))/(2h) = (|h|−|−h|)/(2h) = 0. The limit of this quotient is 0.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now what do you think of Jinwoo's claim?
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The limit of the symmetric quotient exists and equals 0. Whether this means f′(0) exists has to be checked separately by the definition. A student who already knows that |x| bends at 0 can regard this as a counterexample.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The limit 0 exists, so the claim is right, and we confirm that f′(0)=0
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You treated the existence of the limit of the quotient as the same as the derivative existing. Did you check by finding the one-sided slopes according to the definition?
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: To judge the claim, we must directly check whether f′(0) exists according to the definition
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The graph of |x| bends at 0, so I already know it is not differentiable, and I regard it as a counterexample to the claim
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The limit came out 0, so f passes through x=0 flatly
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You interpreted the symmetric quotient being 0 as the graph being flat. Recall the shape of the graph of |x|.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.info: By the definition, (f(h)−f(0))/h = |h|/h. It is 1 when h is greater than 0 and −1 when h is less than 0, so the right-hand limit is 1 and the left-hand limit is −1, and f′(0) does not exist.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Now what do you judge about Jinwoo's claim and its opposite direction (if f is differentiable, this symmetric quotient's limit equals f′(a))?
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.after: |x| is a counterexample, so Jinwoo's claim is false. Conversely, if f is differentiable at x=a, the symmetric quotient can be seen as the average of two slope quotients, so it goes to f′(a). Truth and falsity differ by direction.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The claim is right, and |x| is a special exception that can be ignored
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You missed that one counterexample brings down the claim. The claim is a statement about 'all f'.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The claim is false. The opposite direction must be considered separately
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Both directions are false, so this quotient has nothing to do with the derivative
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You thought a counterexample in one direction also brings down the other direction. Calculate separately what this quotient becomes when f is differentiable.
y-m-62-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The claim is false (counterexample |x|). For the opposite direction, if f is differentiable, we can check that seeing the quotient as the average of (f(a+h)−f(a))/h and (f(a−h)−f(a))/(−h) gives f′(a)
y-m-62-04.s.s1.reflect: How did your confidence in the claim differ between the first (x²) and the last (|x|)? How is 'the example was right' different from 'it holds in all cases'?
y-m-62-04.s.s2.prompt: Restate Jinwoo's claim for him correctly. Use a counterexample to explain why the claim does not hold.
y-m-62-04.s.s2.hint.0: You may reuse the functions and numbers used in the 3 steps of data above.
y-m-62-04.s.s2.hint.1: First write 'the limit exists but f′(0) does not' in one sentence.
y-m-62-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Just because that limit exists, ...
y-m-62-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: In my counterexample, did I show both that the limit of the symmetric quotient exists and that f′(a) does not exist?
y-m-62-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish that the opposite direction 'if differentiable, this limit is f′(a)' does hold?
y-m-62-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check the numbers of the counterexample (0, 1, −1) yourself?
y-m-62-04.s.s2.model.0: You can't say it's differentiable just because the limit of the symmetric quotient exists. If f(x)=|x| and a=0, the quotient is always 0, so the limit is 0, but the right slope is 1 and the left is −1, so f′(0) does not exist.
y-m-62-04.s.s2.model.1: Conversely, if it is differentiable, this limit equals f′(a), but not the other way around. For example, the absolute value function bends at 0 and is not differentiable because the left and right slopes differ, yet this limit is 0.

y-m-62-05.title: How many tangent lines can be drawn from a point not on the curve?
y-m-62-05.topic: Tangent lines drawn from a point outside the curve
y-m-62-05.goal: For a tangent line drawn from a point not on the curve, the point of tangency is unknown, so you must treat it as an unknown and set up conditions; confirm with an example you build yourself that there can be several tangent lines.
y-m-62-05.material: There is a curve y=x² (x is a real number) and a point P(1, −3). If the x-coordinate of the point of tangency is t, the point of tangency is (t, t²), and the slope of the tangent line there is 2t, obtained by plugging x=t into the derivative 2x of y=x². We want to find the t that makes this tangent line pass through point P.
y-m-62-05.thinking.0: Tell apart the roles of the point of tangency and the point the line passes through
y-m-62-05.thinking.1: Set up the conditions as equations
y-m-62-05.thinking.2: Find several solutions and judge how many there are
y-m-62-05.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-05.prereq.1: The relationship between the derivative and the slope of a tangent line
y-m-62-05.prereq.2: The equation of a tangent line (at the point (t, f(t)) on the curve, y−f(t)=f′(t)(x−t))
y-m-62-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct way to write as an equation the condition 'the tangent line at the point of tangency (t, t²) passes through point P(1, −3)'.
y-m-62-05.s.s1.hint.0: In the tangent line equation y−t²=2t(x−t), plug in the coordinates of point P in the places of x and y.
y-m-62-05.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the left side of the equation you plugged into is y−(the y-coordinate of the point of tangency) and the right side is slope×(x−the x-coordinate of the point of tangency).
y-m-62-05.s.s1.r.a: This is an expression that treats P as a point on the curve and uses f(1)=1 in the place of the y-coordinate. P is not the point of tangency.
y-m-62-05.s.s1.r.b: Check the order of x−t when plugging x=1, y=−3 into the tangent line equation y−t²=2t(x−t).
y-m-62-05.s.s1.r.d: This sets the slope of the tangent line to 2. The slope changes with the position t of the point of tangency.
y-m-62-05.s.s1.explain: The equation of the tangent line is y−t²=2t(x−t). If it passes through point P(1, −3), plugging in x=1, y=−3 gives −3−t²=2t(1−t).
y-m-62-05.s.s2.prompt: Make two different tangent lines through point P, each given by the x-coordinate t of its point of tangency and its slope m.
y-m-62-05.s.s2.hint.0: In the equation in c2, plug in one value for t and calculate whether the equality holds.
y-m-62-05.s.s2.hint.1: You can change t and compare the two sides of the equation, or rearrange the equation as an equation in t and solve it.
y-m-62-05.s.s2.var.t: The x-coordinate t of the point of tangency
y-m-62-05.s.s2.var.m: The slope m of that tangent line
y-m-62-05.s.s2.ok.c1: The slope equals the derivative 2t at the point of tangency.
y-m-62-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The slope m differs from the derivative 2t at the point of tangency.
y-m-62-05.s.s2.ok.c2: This tangent line passes through point P(1, −3).
y-m-62-05.s.s2.fail.c2: This tangent line does not pass through point P(1, −3). Check the y value when x=1.
y-m-62-05.s.s2.explain: Rearranging −3−t²=2t(1−t) gives t²−2t−3=0, that is, (t−3)(t+1)=0, so t=3 or t=−1. There are two tangent lines: slope 6 (point of tangency (3, 9)) and slope −2 (point of tangency (−1, 1)).
y-m-62-05.s.s3.prompt: Compare the tangent line drawn at the point (1, 1) on the curve and the tangent lines drawn from point P(1, −3). Where are the points of tangency, how many tangent lines are there in each case, and why do they differ? Write it in one or two sentences.
y-m-62-05.s.s3.hint.0: The slope at (1, 1) can be found by plugging x=1 into the derivative of y=x². Check whether this point is on the curve.
y-m-62-05.s.s3.hint.1: For P, bring in the points of tangency you made in s2 and compare.
y-m-62-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that at a point on the curve, that point is the point of tangency?
y-m-62-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write that P is not on the curve, so the points of tangency must be found separately?
y-m-62-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you take the number of tangent lines from the calculation results (t=3, t=−1)?
y-m-62-05.s.s3.model.0: (1, 1) is a point on the curve, so that point is the point of tangency and there is one tangent line (slope 2). P is not on the curve, so the points of tangency must be found separately, and t=3 and t=−1 come out, so there are two tangent lines.
y-m-62-05.s.s3.model.1: The point the tangent line passes through and the point of tangency are different. At a point on the curve, the two are the same, so the tangent line is determined as one, but for a point outside the curve like P, there are two points of tangency (x=3, x=−1), so there are two tangent lines too.

y-m-62-06.title: Is a local extremum the same as a maximum? Checking all the way to the ends of the interval
y-m-62-06.topic: Maximum and minimum on a closed interval
y-m-62-06.goal: Build a counterexample to the claim that a local maximum is the maximum on the whole closed interval, and explain that the endpoints of the interval must also be compared as candidates.
y-m-62-06.material: Consider the function f(x)=x³−3x (x cubed minus 3x) on the interval −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. The x with f′(x)=3x²−3=0 are −1 and 1, and f(−1)=2 and f(1)=−2. Hajun said, "On this interval, the maximum of f is the local maximum 2, and the minimum is the local minimum −2."
y-m-62-06.thinking.0: Judge whether a claim is true or false
y-m-62-06.thinking.2: Explain how to avoid leaving out candidates
y-m-62-06.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-06.prereq.1: The points where f′(x)=0 found with the derivative and the table of increase and decrease
y-m-62-06.prereq.2: The meaning of local maximum and local minimum
y-m-62-06.s.s1.prompt: How is it good to judge Hajun's statement before doing more calculation?
y-m-62-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find the values directly at both ends of the interval and compare them, to see whether the local maximum 2 is greater than f(x) for all x in the interval.
y-m-62-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether there might be x, other than the positions of the local extrema, that can make f(x) largest in the interval.
y-m-62-06.s.s1.o.a: We should also compare the values at the two endpoints of the interval
y-m-62-06.s.s1.o.b: A local maximum is always the maximum of the interval, so it is right
y-m-62-06.s.s1.r.b: You treated the local maximum as the maximum of the whole interval. A local maximum may be the largest value only near that point.
y-m-62-06.s.s1.o.c: A local extremum can't be a maximum or minimum, so it is wrong
y-m-62-06.s.s1.r.c: There are cases where a local extremum is the maximum or minimum. If you exclude local extrema from the start, you miss candidates.
y-m-62-06.s.s1.o.d: There are two local extrema, so we can't judge
y-m-62-06.s.s1.r.d: You thought the number of points blocks the judgment. Think about how to find where the value is largest in the interval.
y-m-62-06.s.s1.explain: A local extremum is just the largest or smallest value in a nearby range. On a closed interval, you must compare the points where f′(x)=0 and both endpoints of the interval as candidates.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.prompt: As counterexamples to Hajun's claim (the maximum is 2), find and enter three different x in the interval −2 ≤ x ≤ 3 for which f(x) is greater than 2.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.hint.0: Find f(3) at the right endpoint x=3 of the interval and compare it with 2.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.hint.1: Change x to values greater than 2 and find from where f(x) exceeds 2.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.ok.c1: x is in the interval −2 ≤ x ≤ 3.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.fail.c1: x is outside the interval −2 ≤ x ≤ 3.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.fail.c2: At this x, f(x)=x³−3x is not greater than 2.
y-m-62-06.s.s2.explain: x³−3x−2=(x−2)(x+1)², so f(x)>2 when x>2 (at x=−1 it is equal). In the interval, 2<x≤3, and at x=3, f(3)=18. So the maximum is not 2.
y-m-62-06.s.s3.prompt: To find the maximum and minimum of f on this interval, write the values at which points you must compare, and why those points. Also write the actual candidate values.
y-m-62-06.s.s3.hint.0: Recall the counterexample from s2 about where f can be largest on −2 ≤ x ≤ 3.
y-m-62-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write all the candidates in a table and put the f values of each side by side.
y-m-62-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Compare the values at the endpoints of the interval and ... Because ...
y-m-62-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the candidates are the four points (−2, −1, 1, 3)?
y-m-62-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you find the candidate values −2, 2, −2, 18 yourself and compare them?
y-m-62-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you notice that the minimum −2 occurs at two points (x=−2 and x=1)?
y-m-62-06.s.s3.model.0: Find and compare the values at both endpoints of the interval, x=−2 and x=3, and at x=−1 and 1, where f′(x)=0. f(−2)=−2, f(−1)=2, f(1)=−2, f(3)=18, so the maximum is 18 and the minimum is −2.
y-m-62-06.s.s3.model.1: If you look only at local extrema, the value can get bigger at the end of the interval, so that's not enough. So you must compare the values at the points that are local extrema and at both ends x=−2 and x=3, and the largest value 18 is the maximum and the smallest value −2 is the minimum. The minimum occurs at two places, x=−2 and x=1.

y-m-62-07.title: What if the denominator approaches 0 but the limit exists?
y-m-62-07.topic: Limits of fractions whose denominator becomes 0, and undetermined coefficients
y-m-62-07.goal: Using the necessary condition that if the limit of a fraction whose denominator goes to 0 exists as a finite value then the numerator also goes to 0, confirm that when the conditions are insufficient the answer is many pairs, and when a condition is added it is determined as one.
y-m-62-07.material: For constants a and b, consider the limit of the fraction (x²+ax+b)/(x−2) as x goes to 2. The denominator x−2 approaches 0 as x approaches 2. For now, all we know is that the limit of this fraction exists as some real value.
y-m-62-07.thinking.0: Find the condition for the limit to exist
y-m-62-07.thinking.1: Build several solutions in a situation where the conditions are insufficient
y-m-62-07.thinking.2: Explain the process by which an added condition determines the solution
y-m-62-07.prereq.0: School-order assumption: H2 in this task is only a difficulty level in the production layout and does not mean it is assigned to any school year. It is intended for students who have already learned the prerequisites below.
y-m-62-07.prereq.1: The meaning of the limit of a function and calculating limit values
y-m-62-07.prereq.2: Limits in cases where factoring and cancelling are possible
y-m-62-07.prereq.3: What the solutions look like when there is one equation for two unknowns
y-m-62-07.s.s1.prompt: When all we know is the condition that the limit exists as a real value, which is the most appropriate statement about a and b?
y-m-62-07.s.s1.hint.0: Observe what happens to the size of the fraction if the value of the numerator approaches a nonzero number as x approaches 2.
y-m-62-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the difference between the case where the value of the numerator goes to a nonzero number and the case where it goes to 0.
y-m-62-07.s.s1.o.a: The denominator approaches 0, so a limit cannot exist for any a, b
y-m-62-07.s.s1.r.a: You thought that when the denominator approaches 0 it always diverges. Check whether, if the numerator also approaches 0, there are cases where cancelling is possible.
y-m-62-07.s.s1.o.b: A limit exists only when a and b are both 0
y-m-62-07.s.s1.r.b: If a=b=0, it becomes x²/(x−2) and the limit does not exist. Plug in and see directly.
y-m-62-07.s.s1.o.c: The numerator must be 0 at x=2, so b is determined by a and a is free
y-m-62-07.s.s1.o.d: Both a and b are determined as single values
y-m-62-07.s.s1.r.d: You thought both unknowns are determined. Count how many equations the condition that the limit exists gives.
y-m-62-07.s.s1.explain: If the denominator goes to 0 and the limit is finite, the numerator must also go to 0. The value of the numerator at x=2, 4+2a+b, must be 0, so b=−4−2a. There is only this one equation, so a is free.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.prompt: Make three different pairs (a, b) for which the limit exists and the limit value is greater than 0.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.hint.0: First pick one a and adjust b so that the numerator is 0 at x=2.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.hint.1: Cancel that fraction and check whether the value of the remaining expression at x=2 is greater than 0.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerator is 0 at x=2 (the value of the numerator at x=2, 4+2a+b, is 0).
y-m-62-07.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerator is not 0 at x=2, so the limit does not exist. Check the value of 4+2a+b.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The limit value (a+4) is greater than 0.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The limit value is not greater than 0. Check the value at x=2 of the remaining expression x+2+a after cancelling.
y-m-62-07.s.s2.explain: If b=−4−2a, then the numerator x²+ax+b=(x−2)(x+2+a), so after cancelling the limit value is 4+a. For this value to be greater than 0, a>−4. Examples: (1, −6) has limit value 5, (0, −4) has limit value 4, (3, −10) has limit value 7.
y-m-62-07.s.s3.prompt: Suppose the information that the limit value is 5 is added. Write what (a, b) becomes, and explain why it was not determined as one at first but is determined now.
y-m-62-07.s.s3.hint.0: Look again in the explanation from s2 at how the value at x=2 of the expression remaining after cancelling relates to the limit value.
y-m-62-07.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how many conditions are needed to determine both unknowns.
y-m-62-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If the limit value is 5, then ... so (a, b)=...
y-m-62-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write that the limit value 5 gives the equation 'the value a+4 after cancelling and plugging in x=2 is 5'?
y-m-62-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write separately the equation given by the first condition and the equation given by the new condition?
y-m-62-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check the value b=−6 from the condition that the numerator is 0 at x=2?
y-m-62-07.s.s3.model.0: If the limit value is 5, then a+4=5, so a=1, and the numerator must be 0, so 4+2+b=0 and b=−6. At first there was one equation, so a was free, but now there are two equations, so both unknowns are determined.
y-m-62-07.s.s3.model.1: (a, b)=(1, −6). The condition that the limit exists gives only one equation, and the limit value being 5 gives one more equation, a+4=5, so now there are two conditions and it is determined as one.
